name: Exchange Coffee House

documented_range.note: THE YEAR IS DOCUMENTED TWICE IN ANDREAS AND THE MONTH IS NOT. In his hotel chapter: 'Mr. Beaubien had meanwhile built a new house on the northwest corner of Wells and Lake streets. In August of 1834, Mr. and Mrs. Murphy took charge of this new hotel, which they christened the Exchange Coffee House.' In his life of Mark Beaubien: 'In the latter year [1834] he completed another house on the northwest corner of Wells and Lake streets, which was called the Exchange Coffee House, and first kept by Mr. and Mrs. John Murphy.' So the house was finished and trading by August 1834, eleven months before the scene date, and 1834-01-01 is the first day the attested year permits rather than a date anybody gives - which is why this range is inferred and not documented. THE SCENE DATE IS NOT AT RISK: whatever month in 1834 the building went up, it was open under the Murphys from August 1834 and they 'remained there until 1836'. THE END IS A BOUND WHERE THE EVIDENCE STOPS, NOT A DEMOLITION: the Murphys left for the old Sauganash in 1836 and this project has nothing dating the building's fate. Andreas's list of minor houses in 1845 includes 'the Illinois Exchange, corner Wells and Lake streets', which may be the same fabric under a later sign or may not; the phase is closed at the end of the attested tenancy rather than run on speculatively.

position.symbolic_location: North-west corner of Lake Street and Wells Street (today West Lake Street at North Wells Street), fronting south onto Lake.
position.note:
PLACED 2026-08-11. THE CORNER IS DOCUMENTED TWICE IN ANDREAS, IN TWO DIFFERENT CHAPTERS, AND THE COORDINATE IS DERIVED - so the tag follows the weaker half. 'a new house on the northwest corner of Wells and Lake streets' (hotel chapter) and 'another house on the northwest corner of Wells and Lake streets' (life of Mark Beaubien). drloih_hotels agrees. METHOD, the project's standard one: Lake Street and Wells Street both survive on their 1830 plat lines, and the modern West Lake Street / North Wells Street intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap at EPSG:26916 E 447404.02, N 4637283.94 (OSM node 258957316, fetched 2026-08-11). The building's south face is set on the Lake Street frontage 12.2 m north of that centre and its east face on the Wells frontage 12.2 m west of it, 12.2 m being half of an 80 ft street as annotated on Hathaway 1834; the stored coordinate is the polygon origin AFTER the 180 degree facade bearing, which under the renderer's convention (renderers/web/js/walker.js) puts it at the building's north-east corner. Currey has the 1830 Thompson plat laying streets 'uniformly 66 feet wide', which would move each offset 2.1 m - the discrepancy recorded in docs/RESEARCH/hogan_store.md section 5. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M, which is the georeference's residual (data/datum.json: 17.5 m RMS on Wright 1834), not an additional guess. Facade bearing 180, due south onto Lake Street. THAT BEARING IS THE WEAKEST THING HERE: no source says which street the house fronted, and a corner house whose name is an EXCHANGE and whose office booked stage seats could as well have turned its front to Wells. Lake is chosen because it was one of the town's two principal thoroughfares and because the building's neighbours on this record's own street line - the Green Tree three blocks west, the Sauganash two blocks west - front their long side to Lake. THE GROUND UNDER IT IS MODELLED and the building lands on it within the walker's 0.35 m step-up rule, so the phase carries no ground_contact declaration. Note that this footprint would have sat exactly on the OLD box edge - local E +305.1 to +319.1 against an edge at +320 - and that the e1834_harbor_cut heightfield has since been extended to E +1700, which is what puts real terrain under the rest of this parcel too.

THE CORNER IS RULED, 2026-09-26 (T-1604), AND THIS POSITION DOES NOT MOVE. T-1600 recorded a conflict on this record the day before — that Russell E. Heacock's advertisement puts this house one block west, at Lake and Franklin — and the conflict does not survive being read against the claim it came from. The advertisement is chicago_democrat_1835_07_08#c012, and what it places is HEACOCK'S OWN OFFICE and not this building: '[Office in the 2d st]ory, opposite the Ex[cha]n[ge], [corne]r of Lake and Franklin-sts.' The corner clause is the advertiser's address — the one thing a notice like this exists to give — and the Exchange stands in it as the landmark opposite. NOTE ALSO WHAT THE PAPER PRINTS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT: the surviving type reads 'the Ex[cha]n[ge]', not 'the Exchange Coffee House'; the longer form was the reader's expansion, and the note T-1600 wrote quoted the expansion back as though it were the page. THIS PROJECT'S OWN REGISTER ALREADY READ IT THE RULED WAY, which is what settles it: the claim's `business.placement` records `class: corner` with `anchor: 'the Exchange'`, and data/businesses/biz_russell_e_heacock.json carries one anchored location at the franklin+lake crossing with `structure_id: null` and the register's `action: new_building` — Heacock at that corner, in no roof this town holds. So the disagreement was between two READINGS of one advertisement, not between two sources about one building, and Andreas's north-west corner of Wells and Lake — twice, in two chapters, with drloih_hotels agreeing — is unopposed. WHAT THE RULING COSTS, STATED RATHER THAN TIDIED: 'opposite' must then reach from the Franklin corner to this house, about one block of Lake Street. It reaches if Heacock's second story stood on the SOUTH side of Lake at Franklin, because the block face across Lake from there runs Franklin to Wells and this house holds its east end; it does not reach if he stood on the north side, and then 'opposite' is the loose usage for the way across the street. Nothing in the notice says which side he was on and nothing here chooses — both readings leave this corner where Andreas put it, which is why the residual does not touch the coordinate. THE TAG IS UNCHANGED AT `inferred` AND THE SOURCE LIST IS UNCHANGED: the ruling removes an objection and adds no witness to the coordinate, which is still derived from a modern intersection centre. The advertisement is evidence about Heacock's office, and it is cited on that record.

derivation.reason: This placement predates the derivation module. Its provenance and reasoning are recorded in position.note, but no machine-checkable derivation block has been authored for it yet.

footprint.note: INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS BUILDING ANY DIMENSION, a plan, or a room count. 14 x 9 m is about 46 x 30 ft, sized between the Green Tree's 40 x 25 ft - itself derived from a room module rather than measured - and the Western Hotel's attested 40 ft front, on the reasoning that this was Mark Beaubien's second and later house, built in the boom rather than at the forks in 1831, and that it was carrying a hotel and a public room. None of that is evidence about this building. The rectangle is a rectangle because no source describes a plan, and no sources are cited on this attribute because none supports it. TO RESOLVE: the Chicago Democrat and the Chicago American, in both of which this house was a standing address - Dr. Temple's stage line advertised that seats could be taken here - and where a hotel advertisement of the ordinary period kind would count its rooms.

construction.note: NOT ATTESTED, AND IT ALSO CHOSE THE ARCHETYPE, so if it is wrong the building is wrong in kind and not merely in detail. Andreas says Beaubien 'built' and 'completed' a house and never says what of. THE ARGUMENT FOR FRAME: every Chicago hotel this dataset can date to 1833 or later is frame - the Green Tree of 1833, the Tremont of 1833, the Western of 1834-35 - while the log taverns at the forks all belong to the 1828-31 generation; by 1834 the town had sawn lumber, carpenters and a building boom. THE ARGUMENT AGAINST TREATING THAT AS EVIDENCE is this project's own line, docs/LIBERTIES.md L18: the ordinary reading of a TYPE is not evidence about a BUILDING - and the man who built this one had built his last hotel by adding a frame block onto a log cabin. Braced rather than balloon is a second guess inside the first: balloon framing was developed in Chicago in 1832-33, so an 1834 building could be either, and braced is the conservative reading. Both are declared and tagged rather than defaulted.

stories.note: NOT ATTESTED. Two storeys is what a town hotel of 1834 carried and no source says it of this one. Chosen rather than derived. The comparison worth keeping in view is the Tremont, where the one storey count in circulation turns out to be a modern editor's sentence; here there is not even that.

wall_height_m.note: NOT ATTESTED. 5.2 m is about 17 ft - two storeys at period floor heights plus structure and a sill, the same figure this project uses for the Steamboat Hotel and the Miller house's two-storey range. It inherits the storey count above, which is itself a guess.

roof_type.note: NOT ATTESTED. Gable is the ordinary roof for a frame block of this type and period and nothing says it of this building.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 38 degrees is this archetype's mid-range for period framing, inferred from construction practice rather than measured - the same value and the same reasoning as the other frame records here. It is an inference about how a roof of this kind was framed, sitting on a roof form the record has already tagged as a guess.

paint.note: NOT ATTESTED EITHER WAY, and this attribute is read by the archetype, so leaving it out would have painted the building white by default - which is a claim. THERE IS ONE REASON TO WONDER, and it is not enough to act on: the man who built this house had built the white two-storey Sauganash with bright blue shutters that Wau-Bun calls 'the admiration of all the little circle at Wolf Point', so a painted front would be in character. Nothing says he painted this one, and unpainted is the cheaper reading for a speculative-boom house. Still a choice.

gallery.note: NOT ATTESTED EITHER WAY. False is what the archetype falls back to, not a finding - the consequence docs/LIBERTIES.md L19 records for the Green Tree and the Western, that a plain front reads as the answer while a drawn shape at least announces itself as a choice. A coffee house on a main-street corner at which stage seats were booked is exactly the type that often carried a porch over its door.

chimneys.note: Not attested. Two is the count a frame block of this frontage carries if it is heating a public room, a dining room and lodging rooms through a Chicago winter, and it is what this project's other frame hotels record. The COUNT is the inference; position, size and material are the archetype's - docs/LIBERTIES.md L26.

siding_exposure_m.note: INVENTED WITHIN A STOCK SET, NOT DERIVED. No source states the exposed face of any Chicago building's siding. The value is one of four period mill sidings — 4.5, 5, 5.5 or 6 in to the weather; this record wears 5 in — dealt by tools/deal_siding_stock.py: keyed to the phase's construction season, because buildings sided from the same season's shipments of St Joseph sawn lumber tend toward one stock, then advanced so no frame building within 60 m shares this one's. The separation is the surface variety T-0049 reconstructs, not a claim about 1835. docs/LIBERTIES.md L148 owns the invention.

phases.change_note: The house Mark Beaubien built at Lake and Wells in 1834 after leaving the Sauganash, in the state it stood on the scene date and under the keepers it had then. Nothing in the phase is a change of fabric: the christening as the Exchange Coffee House in August 1834, the arrival of Abram A. Markle's name on it by 1836 and the later sign 'Illinois Exchange' are changes of use and of sign.

function.note:
Andreas calls it a hotel in terms - 'Mr. and Mrs. Murphy took charge of this NEW HOTEL, which they christened the Exchange Coffee House' - and lists it in his index among the early hotels. A coffee house of this period is a public house that lodges and feeds people, not a modern cafe. THE STAGE OFFICE IS THE PART THIS PROJECT HAS BEEN GETTING SLIGHTLY WRONG, AND THE CORRECTION IS A YEAR. data/exclusions.json excludes a separate Frink & Walker stage office on the ground that 'in 1835-36 stage seats were taken at Markle's Exchange Coffee House at Lake and Wells', and docs/research/04-structures-south.md line 144 says the same. The sentence behind it is Andreas on Dr John T. Temple's stage line: 'An advertisement that appeared in the American on AUGUST 6, 1836, specifies that John T. Temple & Co. are proprietors of a stage line from Chicago to Peoria ... and that seats can be taken at Markle's Exchange Coffee House.' That is thirteen months AFTER the scene date. Temple's line itself is older - it carried the mail to Ottawa from 1 January 1834 - so seats were being sold somewhere in 1835; nothing reached says where. The exclusion of a separate stage-office BUILDING stands on its own feet, since no such building is attested before 1840. What does not stand is the claim that this house was the stage office in 1835, and this record does not make it.

THE SCENE-YEAR PRESS ATTESTS THE PUBLIC ROOM DIRECTLY, WHERE ANDREAS ONLY RECALLS THE HOUSE. 'a large and respectable Meeting of the Democratic friends of the National Administration of the town of Chicago, was hel[d] at the Ex[change] Coffee House in said town, on Tuesday Evening, April 13, 1835' — the Chicago Democrat of 20 May 1835, page 1 column 3, claim chicago_democrat_1835_05_20#c001, printing the proceedings with Col. T. J. V. Owen calling the meeting to order and Hiram Hugunin in the chair. The secretaries and the committee lists are not repeated here: the reading mints no one off them, and a name written into the town on a building's record is a name the inferred-household deal may no longer use. The same party met here again for the town-election caucus of 6 June 1835 and had moved to the Eagle Coffee House, Trowbridge's, by 24 June. So the house is in business either side of the scene date and its largest room is the town's political one in the spring of 1835, which is a use a tavern_inn function covers and an innkeeping one does not say.
AND THE ADVERTISEMENT IN THE FOLLOWING WEEK'S PAPER NAMES THIS HOUSE AS A LANDMARK, WHICH IS THE WHOLE OF WHAT IT DOES TO IT. Russell E. Heacock advertises an office '[in the 2d st]ory, opposite the Ex[cha]n[ge], [corne]r of Lake and Franklin-sts' (chicago_democrat_1835_07_08#c012). Read once as putting THIS house at Lake and Franklin, that looked like a conflict with Andreas's corner and was recorded as one on 2026-09-26 (T-1600). T-1604 ruled it the next day: the corner in the notice is Heacock's own address and the Exchange is the landmark opposite it, which is how the claim's own placement block and the business register had read it all along. The position does not move, and the reasoning — including what the ruling leaves unresolved about the word 'opposite' — is in position.note above.

occupants.note: Attested twice in Andreas, in two chapters, with dates either side of the scene date: 'In August of 1834, Mr. and Mrs. Murphy took charge of this new hotel, which they christened the Exchange Coffee House. They remained there until 1836, when they removed to the old Sauganash, the name of which they changed to United States Hotel'; and, in the life of Mark Beaubien, the house was 'first kept by Mr. and Mrs. John Murphy'. So 1835-07-01 falls inside their tenancy with eleven months either side, which makes this the best-attested occupancy in the parcel. A CONFLICT WORTH RECORDING RATHER THAN RESOLVING: this project's dossiers have Abram A. Markle 'associated from 1835-36' with the house, and the American's advertisement of August 1836 does call it 'Markle's Exchange Coffee House'. Andreas has Markle taking the MANSION HOUSE in 1835 and keeping it two years. Either Markle held both houses, or one of the two datings is loose; the Murphy tenancy is the one with dates on both sides of the scene date and it is what this record carries.

research_note:
MARK BEAUBIEN'S SECOND HOTEL, DOCUMENTED IN EVERYTHING EXCEPT ITS FABRIC. Two independent passages of Andreas - the hotel chapter and the life of Beaubien - agree on the builder, the corner, the year, the keepers and the name, which is more agreement than any other building in this parcel gets. Not one of them says what it was made of, how big it was, how many storeys it had or what it looked like, so every attribute of the form below is conjectural and the confidence view renders the whole house as massing. THE ARCHETYPE CHOICE IS THEREFORE THE GUESS, and it is argued at form.construction rather than buried in the filename. WHY THERE IS NO SEPARATE STAGE OFFICE IN THIS SCENE: data/exclusions.json already excludes one, and this record deliberately does not replace it with a stage-office function here - the only dated evidence for seats being taken at this house is a Chicago American advertisement of 6 August 1836, and the project's own summary of it as '1835-36' is a year generous. See the function note. TWO NAMES IN THE aka LIST POST-DATE THE SCENE and are carried only so the record can be found under them: 'Markle's Exchange Coffee House' is the 1836 advertisement's form, and 'Illinois Exchange' is how Andreas lists a house at this corner among the minor houses of 1845. A SCENE-LEVEL CHECK ON THE PARCEL AS A WHOLE: the Chicago American of 15 August 1835, quoted by Andreas, counted 'eight taverns' in the town six weeks after the scene date. With this record, the Tremont and the Mansion House added, the dataset holds exactly eight public houses for 1835. See docs/RESEARCH/exchange_coffee_house.md.

THE CORNER, RULED 2026-09-26 (T-1604): THE ADVERTISEMENT PLACES THE LAWYER, NOT THE HOUSE. T-1600 opened a source conflict here on 2026-09-25 — Andreas's north-west corner of Wells and Lake, twice and corroborated by drloih_hotels, against Russell E. Heacock's advertisement in the Chicago Democrat, which was read as putting this house at the corner of Lake and Franklin, the adjoining block west. THERE IS NO CONFLICT. The notice (chicago_democrat_1835_07_08#c012) reads '[Office in the 2d st]ory, opposite the Ex[cha]n[ge], [corne]r of Lake and Franklin-sts', and the corner in it is the address of the OFFICE being advertised; this house appears as the landmark opposite. The claim's own `business.placement` says so — `class: corner`, `anchor: 'the Exchange'` — and data/businesses/biz_russell_e_heacock.json already seats Heacock at the franklin+lake crossing with `structure_id: null`, the register's `new_building`. So what looked like two sources disagreeing about one building was two readings of one advertisement disagreeing with each other, and the one that reached this record had re-attached the corner from the advertiser to his landmark. A SECOND THING THE RULING CORRECTS: the page prints 'the Ex[cha]n[ge]', not 'the Exchange Coffee House' — the fuller name was expansion, and it should not be quoted as the paper's words. WHAT IS LEFT OVER, AND IT IS NOT NOTHING: 'opposite' has to carry about one block of Lake Street to reach this corner. It does so on the reading that puts Heacock's second story on the south side of Lake at Franklin, facing the block face that runs Franklin to Wells with this house at its east end; on the north side it is loose usage. The notice does not say which, so neither does this record, and the position is unmoved either way and still tagged inferred. The 1835-05-20 reading's own note carried the same mis-attachment and is corrected with this ruling. ONE JOB FALLS OUT OF IT: the anchor the paper prints is 'the Exchange', and the register resolves an anchor against the committed town by WHOLE-SET equality of identity-bearing words (T-0406), so {exchange} does not equal this record's {exchange, coffee, house} and the printed anchor resolves to no building here. That is a separate piece of work and is filed as one; nothing about it is settled by adding an aka on this ruling's way past.


THE SHORT NAME IS RULED IN, 2026-09-26 (T-1607): THIS HOUSE ANSWERS TO ‘the Exchange’, AND THAT AKA IS OF THE SCENE YEAR, unlike the two above it. The register resolves a printed landmark against the committed town by WHOLE-SET equality of identity-bearing words (T-0406, ruled on the Tremont), so the paper's bare ‘the Exchange’ — the word set {exchange} — reached neither this record's name nor either later aka, and it named nothing the town held. THE CORPUS EQUATES THE TWO FORMS ITSELF, AND DOES IT TWICE. Russell E. Heacock's standing advertisement sets the full form on 27 May 1835 — ‘opposite the Exchange Coffee House, corner of Lake and Franklin-sts’, chicago_democrat_1835_05_27#c007 — and the bare one on 8 July — ‘the Exchange’, chicago_democrat_1835_07_08#c012: one advertiser, one office, two settings of one advertisement. J. A. Marshall's dancing-school notice of 19 November 1834 reads ‘one door north of the Exchange’ (chicago_democrat_1834_11_19#c004) and this project already carried its anchor as the full name, so the equation was being made here in silence. WHAT IT RELEASES is Wm. H. Kennicott, surgeon dentist, whose notice prints ‘OFFICE OPPOSITE THE EXCHENGE, LAKF-STRYE’ over two settings (chicago_democrat_1835_08_05#c021, chicago_democrat_1835_08_19#c014) — on Lake Street, which is this house's own street on either reading of the corner. THE MEASURED EFFECT, and it is the whole of it: the businesses this building anchors go 1 → 2 (Marshall, and now Kennicott) and the register's actions move new_building 26 → 27 and street_only 61 → 60. Every other business and all 2,667 person rows re-derive byte-identical. WHAT THE AKA DOES NOT REACH, because the MATCH is unchanged and only this record's own list of names it answers to grew: the Sauganash's ‘Eagle Exchange Tavern’ is {eagle, exchange, tavern}, a SUPERSET, which whole-set matching refuses as it always did — that second house carrying the same word is why the short form was ruled rather than assumed; ‘the Exchange Tavern’ would be a third form and names nothing; and the other coffee houses in Andreas's index (Lincoln's, the Eagle, the Lake Street) are not in the structure layer and none of them is called the Exchange. Three self-test cases in tools/compile_register.py hold all of that shut. THE 1834 TRUSTEES' VENUE MENTIONS ARE UNTOUCHED BY THIS. The board met at ‘the Exchange’ later in 1834, in the list recorded on mansion_house.json that brackets the Graves-to-Haddock handover; those are prose in a note, not anchors in the gazetteer, so the register never resolved them and does not resolve them now. They corroborate that the short name was current in the town, and they stay what that record already calls them — a venue, tracking convenience, and never by itself a tenancy. See docs/RESEARCH/exchange_coffee_house.md § 6.
